title: Maths Showcase
subtitle: One original course that uses every maths feature of gamify-learn V1.5: equations, graphs, proofs, matrices, calculus, probability.
about: Demo and regression test for the maths layer. Original content. If a formula, graph, proof or spot-the-mistake step looks wrong here, it is a bug.

glossary.meaning: An $x$ value where a function equals zero: where its graph meets the x-axis.
$b^2-4ac$. Positive: two real roots. Zero: one. Negative: none.
A straight line through two points of a curve.
The slope of a curve at a point; $f'(x)$ or $\dv{f}{x}$.
The area under a curve: $\int_a^b f(x)\,\dd x$.
For a 2 by 2 matrix, $ad-bc$. The factor by which areas scale.
Flip a matrix over its diagonal: $A\T$.
Your belief $\Pr(H)$ before seeing the evidence.
A proof that shows a first case and that each case implies the next.
$\sigma$: the typical distance of values from the mean.

quests.title: Equations: keep the balance
quests.question: How do you find the unknown in an equation without guessing?
outcomes: Solve a linear equation and show every line
Say WHY each line is allowed
Pick the quicker of two correct strategies
Catch the classic bracket mistake

steps.prompt: A scale balances: 3 identical bags plus 4 loose coins on the left, 19 coins on the right. How many coins are in one bag?
steps.answer: 5 coins. Take the 4 loose coins off BOTH sides (15 coins left), then split the 15 coins between the 3 bags.

steps.title: An equation is a balanced scale
lines: $3x+4=19$ says: three bags of $x$ coins each, plus 4 loose coins, weigh the same as 19 coins.
One rule keeps the scale balanced: **whatever you do to one side, do to the other side.**
The goal is one bag alone on a side: $x=\text{a number}$.
steps.analogy: A see-saw. Add a kilo to one side and it tips. Add a kilo to both sides and it stays level.
steps.intuition: Solving means undoing what was done to $x$, last thing first. Here $x$ was multiplied by 3, then 4 was added. So subtract 4 first, then divide by 3.

steps.title: Solve $3x+4=19$, every line

steps.label: Read the equation
steps.why: Name the pieces first. 3 bags and 4 coins weigh the same as 19 coins.

steps.label: Take off the loose coins
steps.why: Subtracting 4 undoes the +4. It must happen on BOTH sides or the scale tips.

steps.label: Split into one bag
steps.why: Dividing by 3 undoes the 'times 3'. The 3 on the left cancels with the 3 under $3x$.

steps.label: Check by putting 5 back
steps.why: If both sides still match, the answer is right. Always do this; it catches slips.

steps.shortcut: Moving a term across the $=$ flips its sign: $3x=19-4$. It is the same step, written faster.
steps.check: Put your answer back into the ORIGINAL equation, not into a line you rewrote.
steps.trap: Dividing only part of the left side: $\frac{3x+4}{3}$ is not $x+4$. Divide EVERY term, or subtract first.

steps.title: Two correct ways. Which is quicker?
steps.intro: Solve $10(y+2)=6(y+2)+12$. Both ways are right; one is shorter.
rows: 3 lines. Spotting the repeated block is the trick.
steps.keep: Before you start, look at the structure. A repeated block is a hint to treat it as one thing.

steps.title: Find the mistake

steps.label: Line 1
steps.mistake: The 2 multiplies BOTH terms in the bracket: $2(x+3)=2x+6$, not $2x+3$.

steps.label: Line 2
steps.why: The move itself (subtract 3 from both sides) is legal. It only carries the error from line 1 forward.

steps.label: Line 3
steps.why: Dividing both sides by 2 is legal too. The wrong value comes from line 1.

steps.lesson: A number outside a bracket multiplies EVERYTHING inside: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. Check by substituting: $2(4+3)=14$.

steps.title: Your turn 1
hints: You have $x$ on both sides. Get all the $x$ terms on one side first.
Subtract $3x$ from both sides, then add 7 to both sides.

steps.label: Gather the $x$ terms
steps.why: Subtract 3x from both sides so x lives on one side only.

steps.label: Clear the loose number
steps.why: Add 7 to both sides: it undoes the -7.

steps.label: Divide
steps.why: Undo the 'times 2'.

steps.label: Check
steps.why: Both sides give 33.

quiz.q: To solve $x+9=20$ you subtract 9. Why on BOTH sides?
wrong: Only the left side has an x
quiz.why: An equation says two sides are equal. Do the same to both and they stay equal.

quiz.q: What is $x$ in $4x-6=14$?

cards.front: The one rule for solving equations
cards.back: Do the same thing to both sides.
$ab+ac$. The outside number multiplies everything inside.

lines: An equation is a balance: do the same to both sides.
Undo operations in reverse order.
Always check by substituting back.
Spot repeated blocks to shorten the work.
recap.teach: Explain to a friend why we subtract on both sides.

quests.title: Quadratics: roots, curve and formula
quests.question: Where does a U-shaped curve cross zero, and is there a formula that always finds it?
quests.previously: You can solve equations where $x$ appears once. Now $x$ appears squared.
outcomes: Read roots, vertex and intercept off a parabola
Use the quadratic formula without dropping a sign
Predict the number of roots from the discriminant
Follow a derivation line by line

steps.prompt: Throw a ball up and plot its height against time. What shape do you think the graph has, and when is the height zero?
steps.answer: A hill-shaped curve (a parabola). The height is zero at launch and again when the ball lands: two moments, two roots.

steps.title: A quadratic draws a U
lines: A quadratic has an $x^2$ term: $y=ax^2+bx+c$. Its graph is a U-shaped curve called a **parabola**.
The **roots** are the $x$ values where the curve touches $y=0$. Solving $ax^2+bx+c=0$ means finding them.
steps.analogy: Throw a ball: it rises, peaks, falls. Height against time is a parabola. The roots are the moments it is at ground level.

steps.title: The curve $y=x^2-5x+6$

captions.1: The curve meets the x-axis where $y=0$: at $x=2$ and $x=3$. These are the **roots**.
captions.2: The lowest point sits exactly halfway between the roots, at $x=\frac{2+3}{2}=2.5$.
captions.3: At $x=0$ the curve is at $y=6$. That is the constant $c$: the height where the curve cuts the y-axis.

steps.keep: Two roots = the curve crosses the axis twice. The picture and the algebra give the same numbers.

steps.title: The quadratic formula
steps.read: x equals minus b, plus or minus the square root of (b squared minus 4 a c), all over 2 a.

parts.name: a: the x-squared number
parts.plain: The number in front of $x^2$. It sets how wide or narrow the U is, and whether it opens up ($a>0$) or down ($a<0$).

parts.name: b: the x number
parts.plain: The number in front of $x$. Keep its sign: in $x^2-5x+6$, $b=-5$.

parts.name: c: the loose number
parts.plain: The number with no $x$. It is the height where the curve cuts the y-axis.
parts.effect: Moves the whole curve up or down.

parts.name: the discriminant
parts.plain: The number under the square root. It decides how many real roots there are.
parts.effect: Positive: 2 roots. Zero: 1 root. Negative: none (the curve misses the axis).

parts.name: plus-or-minus
parts.plain: Do the sum twice: once with +, once with -. That is where the two roots come from.

steps.trap: Writing $b=5$ when the equation has $-5x$. A lost minus sign gives wrong roots every time. Write $a=\;,\;b=\;,\;c=\;$ with signs first.

steps.title: Solve $x^2-5x+6=0$ with the formula

steps.label: Read off a, b, c
steps.why: Compare with $ax^2+bx+c$. Take each number WITH its sign: $-5x$ means $b=-5$.

steps.label: Discriminant
steps.why: $(-5)^2=25$: a negative squared is positive. The result 1 is positive, so we expect two roots.

steps.label: Square root
steps.why: Easy here; in general leave it as a root if it is not a perfect square.

steps.label: Plug in
steps.why: $-(-5)=+5$: two minus signs make a plus.

steps.label: Do + and - separately
steps.why: The plus-or-minus gives one root each way.

steps.label: Check with the graph
steps.why: These are exactly the points where the graph crossed the axis.

steps.shortcut: When $a=1$, look for two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$ with the opposite sign: $2\times3=6$, $2+3=5$. No formula needed.
steps.check: The roots must match the places the curve crosses the x-axis.

steps.title: Move $a$, $b$, $c$ and watch the roots
steps.intro: The red line is the parabola. Watch the discriminant: when it goes negative the curve floats off the axis.
tries: Set $c=12$ and watch the discriminant turn negative.
Set $a=-1$ and see the U flip upside down.
steps.keep: Discriminant above 0 = two crossings, 0 = touches once, below 0 = never crosses.

steps.title: Where the formula comes from
steps.plan: Rewrite the left side as a perfect square (completing the square), then take square roots.

steps.label: Divide by a
steps.reason: We may divide both sides by $a$ because $a\neq0$. Now $x^2$ has coefficient 1.

steps.label: Add the missing square
steps.reason: Half of $\frac{b}{a}$ is $\frac{b}{2a}$. Adding its square to BOTH sides completes the square.

steps.label: Square root of both sides
steps.reason: A number and its negative both square to the same value, hence $\pm$. $\sqrt{4a^2}=2a$.

steps.label: Isolate x
steps.reason: Subtract b/2a from both sides and combine the fractions.

steps.conclusion: This is the quadratic formula. It works for every a, b, c with a not zero.
steps.keep: The formula is not magic: it is completing the square done once, for all numbers.

steps.title: Your turn 2
hints: Discriminant: $3^2-4(2)(-2)$. Two minus signs make a plus.

steps.label: a, b, c
steps.why: Signs included.

steps.label: Roots
steps.why: Plus and minus each give one root.

quiz.q: For $x^2-4x+4=0$, what is the discriminant $b^2-4ac$?
quiz.why: $(-4)^2-4(1)(4)=16-16=0$. Zero means the curve just touches the axis: one root ($x=2$).

quiz.q: A parabola has discriminant $-7$. How many times does it cross the x-axis?
quiz.why: A negative discriminant needs the square root of a negative number, which is not real. The curve misses the axis.

quiz.q: In $3x^2-8x+1=0$ what is $b$?
quiz.why: b is the number in front of x, with its sign.

quiz.q: What does 'subtract 5 from both sides' keep true?
quiz.why: Same operation on both sides keeps the balance (Quest 1).

cards.front: Discriminant: what does its sign tell you?

cards.back: The $x$ values where the curve meets $y=0$.

lines: A parabola is the graph of a quadratic.
Roots are where $y=0$.
The discriminant counts the roots.
The formula comes from completing the square.
recap.teach: Draw a parabola with two roots and label roots, lowest point, y-intercept.

quests.title: Calculus: slope and area
quests.question: How steep is a curve at one point, and how much area is under it?
quests.previously: You can read a curve's roots. Now we ask how fast it is changing.
outcomes: Explain the derivative as a slope that a secant line approaches
Differentiate powers with a rule you understand
See an integral as a limit of rectangles
Evaluate a simple definite integral

steps.prompt: A car's average speed over a 2-hour trip is 60 km/h. Does that tell you its speed at exactly 1:17 pm? How could you get closer?
steps.answer: No: it only averages. Shrink the time window around 1:17 (say one minute, then one second) and the average gets closer to the exact speed. That shrinking window is the idea of a derivative.

steps.title: Slope of a curve
lines: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve's slope changes from point to point.
Trick: pick two points on the curve and join them with a straight line (a **secant**). Its slope is easy: $\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$.
Now slide the second point closer and closer to the first.
steps.analogy: A car's speedometer: average speed over a long trip is a secant slope. The speedometer reading right now is the tangent slope.

steps.title: From secant to tangent for $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=1$

captions.4: The slopes 4, 3, 2.5, ... head for **2**. The line touching at one point only is the **tangent**; its slope is the **derivative** $f'(1)=2$.

steps.keep: Derivative = the number the secant slopes settle on as the second point slides in.

steps.title: The derivative of $x^2$, from the definition
steps.problem: Find the slope of $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=1$ exactly, using $f'(1)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$.

steps.label: Name the second point
steps.why: $h$ is how far we slide right. A secant needs two points; this gives the second.

steps.label: Expand the square
steps.why: $(1+h)(1+h)$: multiply every term by every term.

steps.label: Subtract 1
steps.why: The +1 and -1 cancel. Everything left has an h.

steps.label: Cancel h
steps.why: Factor h out and cancel. We may because $h\neq0$ while it is only 'very small'.

steps.label: Let h shrink to 0
steps.why: As $h\to0$, the term $h$ vanishes. This matches the slopes 4, 3, 2.5, ... of the picture.

steps.check: At x = 1 the tangent in the graph rises 2 for every 1 step right.

steps.title: The power rule
steps.intro: Doing that limit every time is slow. The pattern is always the same:
steps.read: The derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus 1.

parts.name: x: the variable
parts.effect: The result is a new function of x: the slope at each x.

parts.name: n: the power
parts.effect: It comes down in front, and the power drops by 1.

steps.shortcut: Bring the power down, subtract 1 from it. $x^2\to2x^1=2x$. At $x=1$ that gives 2, matching the limit.
steps.trap: Forgetting to lower the power: the derivative of $x^3$ is $3x^2$, not $3x^3$.

steps.title: Area under $y=x^2$ from 0 to 2

captions.1: Cut the area into 4 strips and use rectangles: left sum $=0.5(0^2+0.5^2+1^2+1.5^2)=1.75$, too small.
captions.2: 16 thinner strips follow the curve more closely. The sum gets closer to the true area.
captions.3: With infinitely many strips the rectangles fill the region exactly. That limit is the **integral** $\int_0^2 x^2\,\dd x$.

steps.keep: Integral = the limit of rectangle areas as the strips get thinner.

steps.title: Evaluate $\int_0^2 x^2\,\dd x$
steps.problem: Find the exact area under $y=x^2$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$.

steps.label: Find an antiderivative
steps.why: We need $F$ with $F'(x)=x^2$. By the power rule, $\dv{(x^3/3)}{x}=\frac{3x^2}{3}=x^2$.

steps.label: Plug in the top and bottom
steps.why: The area equals F(top) minus F(bottom).

steps.label: Simplify
steps.why: Compare with the left sum 1.75 for 4 strips: the exact area is a bit larger, as the picture showed.

steps.title: Your turn 3
hints: Then put x = 2 into the derivative.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.why: The constant 3 stays; the power rule acts on $x^4$.

quiz.q: What is $\dv{x^5}{x}$?
quiz.why: Bring the 5 down, lower the power: $5x^4$.

quiz.q: As the second point slides toward the first, the secant slope approaches...
quiz.why: That limiting value is what we call the derivative.

quiz.q: The discriminant of $x^2+2x+5$ is...
quiz.why: $2^2-4(1)(5)=4-20=-16$. Negative: no real roots.

quiz.q: An integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,\dd x$ is best pictured as...
quiz.answer: The area under the curve from a to b
wrong: The average of a and b
quiz.why: Sum of thin rectangles in the limit.

cards.back: The slope of the curve at one point: the limit of secant slopes.
The area under a curve: the limit of rectangle sums.

lines: Secant slopes settle on the tangent slope: the derivative.
Power rule: $x^n\to n\,x^{n-1}$.
Integral = limit of rectangle areas.
Area $=F(\text{top})-F(\text{bottom})$.
recap.teach: Say in 30 seconds why a derivative is a limit of secant slopes.

quests.title: Vectors and matrices
quests.question: How can a grid of numbers move, stretch and rotate pictures?
quests.previously: You solved for unknown numbers and read slopes. Now a whole table of numbers acts as one machine.
outcomes: Say what a matrix does to the unit square
Multiply matrices entry by entry
Compute a 2 by 2 determinant and inverse
Catch the order-of-transpose mistake

steps.prompt: Stretch a square sheet of rubber to twice its width, same height. By what factor does its area change?
steps.answer: Twice the area. A matrix that stretches x by 2 does exactly this, and its determinant (the area scale) is 2.

steps.title: A matrix is a machine for moving points
lines: Write a point as a column $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$. A $2\times2$ matrix turns it into a new point.
The **first column** says where the point $(1,0)$ lands. The **second column** says where $(0,1)$ lands.
Everything else follows, because every point is some amount of those two steps.
steps.analogy: Two arrows on graph paper, one right and one up. The matrix says where each arrow goes; the rest of the paper is dragged along.

steps.title: Drag the matrix, watch the square
steps.intro: The grey square is the unit square. The blue shape is its image under $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$.
tries: Set $a=0,\,b=-1,\,c=1,\,d=0$: the square turns 90 degrees. The red dot is where $(1,0)$ lands, the green dot where $(0,1)$ lands.
Make the area scale $ad-bc$ equal 0: the square flattens into a line.
steps.keep: Red dot = first column. Green dot = second column. The area scale is the determinant.

steps.title: Matrix times vector
steps.read: Each output entry is a row of the matrix times the column: multiply pairs, then add.

parts.name: top-left
parts.plain: Multiplies x in the new x.

parts.name: top-right
parts.plain: Multiplies y in the new x.

parts.name: bottom-left
parts.plain: Multiplies x in the new y.

parts.name: bottom-right
parts.plain: Multiplies y in the new y.

steps.trap: Row times column, never column times column. The first row makes the first output.

steps.title: Multiply two matrices, entry by entry

steps.label: Top-left: row 1 of A, column 1 of B
steps.why: Multiply matching positions, then add.

steps.label: Top-right: row 1, column 2
steps.why: Same row, next column.

steps.label: Bottom-left: row 2, column 1
steps.why: Next row, first column.

steps.label: Bottom-right: row 2, column 2
steps.why: Last entry.

steps.label: Assemble
steps.why: Compare with A: its columns are swapped. B is the 'swap the columns' matrix.

steps.shortcut: Multiplying on the right by $B$ just rearranges the columns of $A$. Read the columns of $B$ as instructions: 'take column 2, then column 1'.
steps.trap: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: $AB\neq BA$ in general.

steps.title: Determinant and inverse of a 2 by 2

steps.label: Determinant
steps.why: It is the area scale from the lab. Non-zero, so $A$ can be undone.

steps.label: Swap and negate
steps.why: Swap the diagonal entries, flip the sign of the other two, divide by the determinant.

steps.label: Check A times its inverse
steps.why: The identity matrix means the inverse undoes A.

steps.title: Find the mistake

steps.label: Line 1
steps.why: Inner sizes match (3 and 3); the result takes the outer sizes 2 and 2.

steps.label: Line 2
steps.mistake: Transposing a product REVERSES the order. Think of socks and shoes: to undo putting on socks then shoes, take off the shoes first.

steps.label: Line 3
steps.work: $$A\T\text{ is }3\times2,\; B\T\text{ is }2\times3,\text{ so }A\T B\T\text{ is }3\times3$$
steps.why: True, and it exposes the error: $(AB)\T$ is $2\times2$, so it cannot equal a $3\times3$ matrix. A size check catches it.

steps.lesson: Always size-check a matrix identity. A mismatch means the order is wrong.

steps.title: Your turn 4
steps.problem: Rotate the point $(2,3)$ by 90 degrees using $R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

steps.label: Top entry
steps.why: Row 1 of R against the column.

steps.label: Bottom entry
steps.why: Row 2 of R against the column.

steps.label: Result
steps.why: The point moved a quarter turn anticlockwise, as the lab showed.

quiz.q: In a 2 by 2 matrix, the FIRST column tells you...
quiz.why: Columns are the images of the unit steps.

quiz.q: $\det\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}=$
quiz.why: $ad-bc=3\cdot2-1\cdot4=2$.

quiz.q: What is the slope of $f(x)=x^3$ at $x=1$?
quiz.why: Power rule: $3x^2$, at $x=1$ gives 3.

cards.back: Each output entry = a row of the matrix times the column: multiply pairs, add.

lines: Columns of a matrix = where the unit steps land.
Multiply: row against column.
$\det=ad-bc$ is the area scale; zero means the plane is flattened.
Size-check identities.
recap.teach: Describe what the matrix with columns (0,1) and (-1,0) does.

quests.title: Probability, proof and the bell curve
quests.question: How do you update a belief after evidence, and how do you KNOW a rule is always true?
quests.previously: You can compute and transform. Now you decide how sure to be, and prove things.
outcomes: Use Bayes' rule with natural frequencies
Follow a proof by cases and by induction
Read the 68-95 rule off a bell curve
Count choices with a binomial coefficient

steps.prompt: A medical test catches 90% of ill people, and 1 person in 100 is ill. You test positive. Is the chance you are ill about 90%, 50% or 15%? Guess before you calculate.
steps.answer: About 15%. Most people guess 90%. We will see why in the next few screens.

steps.title: Bayes' rule
steps.intro: How likely is a hypothesis H after you see evidence E?
steps.read: The probability of H given E equals the probability of E given H, times the prior probability of H, divided by the probability of E.

parts.name: H: the hypothesis
parts.plain: The thing you want to know, e.g. 'the person is ill'.
parts.effect: Pr(H) is your belief BEFORE the evidence (the prior).

parts.name: E: the evidence
parts.plain: What you observed, e.g. 'the test is positive'.
parts.effect: Pr(E) is how common the evidence is overall.

steps.trap: Mixing up $\Pr(H\given E)$ with $\Pr(E\given H)$. A test that catches 90% of the ill does not mean 90% of positives are ill.

steps.title: A positive test: how worried should you be?
steps.problem: 1% of people have a condition. The test is positive for 90% of ill people and also for 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Probability you are ill?

steps.label: Imagine 1000 people
steps.why: Whole people are easier to picture than percentages (natural frequencies).

steps.label: Who tests positive?
steps.why: Apply each test rate to its own group.

steps.label: Positives in total
steps.why: This is $\Pr(E)$ counted in people.

steps.label: Fraction of positives who are ill
steps.why: Of everyone who tests positive, only 9 are really ill.

steps.intuition: The condition is rare, so false alarms from the large healthy group swamp the true positives.
steps.check: The answer must be below 100% and, with a rare condition, far below the test's 90% rate.

steps.title: Prove $|x|\geq x$
steps.plan: A number is either not negative or negative. Check the claim in each case.

steps.label: Case 1: $x\ge0$
steps.reason: By the definition, the first line applies, and a number is equal to itself.

steps.label: Case 2: $x<0$
steps.reason: By the definition, $|x|=-x$. Since $x$ is negative, $-x$ is positive, and positive numbers exceed negative ones.

steps.conclusion: Every real number falls in one of the two cases, and both give the claim.
steps.keep: Proof by cases: split into cases that cover everything, then prove each.

steps.title: The first n odd numbers add up to n squared
steps.plan: Like dominoes: show the first falls, then show that any domino that falls knocks over the next.

steps.label: Base case, n = 1
steps.reason: The first domino falls: the claim holds for n = 1.

steps.label: Assume it for n = k
steps.reason: Induction hypothesis: suppose domino k has fallen.

steps.label: Add the next odd number
steps.reason: Add the same thing, $2k+1$, to both sides of the hypothesis.

steps.label: That is the claim for k + 1
steps.reason: Domino k+1 falls whenever domino k does.

steps.conclusion: The first domino falls and each knocks over the next, so the claim holds for every n.
steps.trap: Skipping the base case. Without a first fallen domino, nothing falls.

steps.title: The bell curve and the 68-95 rule

captions.1: About **68%** of values fall within 1 standard deviation $\sigma$ of the mean $\mu$.
captions.2: About **95%** fall within $2\sigma$. Only 5% are further out.

steps.intuition: The curve is the density: area = probability. The total area is 1.

steps.title: Your turn 5
steps.problem: A club must choose 2 of 5 people for a team. How many different pairs are possible?
hints: Order does not matter, so use $\binom{5}{2}=\dfrac{5!}{2!\,3!}$.

steps.label: Write the coefficient
steps.why: $\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ counts ways to choose k of n.

steps.label: Cancel
steps.why: $5!=5\cdot4\cdot3!$, so the $3!$ appears top and bottom.

quiz.q: 1000 people, 1% ill. Test: 90% of ill and 5% of healthy test positive. Roughly how many positives are ill?
quiz.why: 9 ill positives against 49.5 healthy positives.

quiz.q: In an induction proof, what is the 'base case' for?
quiz.answer: To show the first statement is true
quiz.why: Without a true first domino, the chain never starts.

quiz.q: About what share of a normal distribution lies within $2\sigma$ of the mean?
quiz.why: The 68-95-99.7 rule: 95% lies within two standard deviations. 68% is only one standard deviation; 99.7% is three.

quiz.q: What is the slope of $f(x)=4x^2$ at $x=3$?

cards.back: Show the first case. Show that if case k holds, case k+1 holds.

lines: Bayes: update with natural frequencies.
Proofs: cases cover everything; induction = dominoes.
Normal: 68% within 1 sigma, 95% within 2 sigma.
recap.teach: Explain why a positive test for a rare condition is often a false alarm.

quests.title: Capstone: mixed problems
quests.question: Can you pick the right tool when nobody tells you which one?
quests.previously: Five tools: equations, quadratics, calculus, matrices, probability. Now they arrive mixed.
outcomes: Choose a strategy before computing
Show every line with its reason
Check each answer

steps.prompt: Before solving $4(x-1)=2(x-1)+10$: which strategy is faster, opening the brackets or treating $(x-1)$ as one block?
steps.answer: The block. $(x-1)$ appears on both sides, so subtract $2(x-1)$ and you are left with $2(x-1)=10$.

steps.label: Treat (x-1) as a block
steps.why: The block appears on both sides, so subtract it once.

steps.label: Undo the times 2
steps.why: Divide both sides by 2.

steps.label: Undo the minus 1
steps.why: Add 1 to both sides.

steps.label: Check
steps.why: Both sides agree.

steps.title: Mixed 2: when does it land?
steps.problem: A ball's height in metres is $h=-t^2+4t+5$. At what time $t>0$ does it hit the ground ($h=0$)?
hints: Set $h=0$ and multiply by $-1$ to make $a=1$.

steps.label: Set h = 0
steps.why: Multiplying both sides by -1 keeps the balance and makes a = 1.

steps.label: Discriminant
steps.why: Positive, so two roots.

steps.label: Roots
steps.why: Plus and minus each give one root.

steps.label: Choose the sensible one
steps.why: A negative time is before the throw, so it does not apply.

steps.title: Mixed 3: area
steps.problem: Find the area under $y=x^2$ from $x=0$ to $x=3$.

steps.label: Antiderivative
steps.why: Its derivative is x squared (power rule backwards).

steps.label: Top minus bottom
steps.why: Area = F(3) - F(0).

steps.title: Mixed 4: matrix
steps.problem: $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Where do $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ land, and by what factor does area change?
hints: The columns of S are the images of the unit steps.

steps.label: Read the columns
steps.why: First column = image of (1,0); second column = image of (0,1).

steps.label: Determinant
steps.why: The unit square (area 1) becomes a 2 by 3 rectangle (area 6).

steps.answer: Stretch x by 2 and y by 3; area scales by 6.

quiz.q: $6(a+1)=4(a+1)+8$. What is the cleverest first move?
quiz.why: The block (a+1) is on both sides. Opening brackets also works but takes more lines.

quiz.q: The parabola $y=x^2+1$ ... crosses the x-axis how many times?
quiz.why: Discriminant $0-4=-4<0$, and the curve never drops below $y=1$.

quiz.q: The area under $y=2x$ from 0 to 3 is...
quiz.why: Antiderivative $x^2$: $3^2-0^2=9$. It is also a triangle: $\frac12\cdot3\cdot6=9$.

quiz.q: A matrix with $\det=0$ ...
quiz.answer: Flattens the plane onto a line
quiz.why: Area scale 0 means every shape collapses; there is no inverse.

quiz.q: A test is positive for 99% of ill people, but the condition affects 1 in 10,000. A positive result mostly means...
quiz.answer: A false alarm is still more likely than being ill
quiz.why: With a tiny prior, healthy people far outnumber ill ones, so false positives dominate (Bayes' rule).

quiz.q: In a proof by induction, the step 'if it holds for k, it holds for k + 1' alone is not enough because...
quiz.answer: Nothing says the first case is true
wrong: It only works for even numbers
quiz.why: The base case starts the chain; the step passes it along.

quiz.q: Values are normally distributed with mean 100 and $\sigma=10$. About 95% lie between...
quiz.why: 95% lies within $2\sigma$: $100\pm20$. 90 to 110 is only $1\sigma$ (68%); 70 to 130 is $3\sigma$.
